utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. May I remind the witness of the affirmation that he took at the commencement of his evidence. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic: Continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Samardzic. I will continue where I left off. Mr. Samardzic, can you please tell us how many days ago you arrived in The Hague to testify before this Court?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe about 15 days ago, or 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you reread your statement, the one you gave to the investigators, before you faced the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the written statement you provided to the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did reread it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, then, please tell me when it was that you drew the investigators' attention to the fact that there were corrections to be made to your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived, or one of those days, that's when I told them. However, even as early as testifying against Slobodan Milosevic, I drew the investigators' attention to certain corrections that needed to be made. I pointed out errors that I thought should be corrected, as well as discrepancies. We're not talking about now; we're talking about perhaps two years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean probably in the course of your testimony in the Milosevic case, you suggested certain amendments?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what exactly you pointed out?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several of those that related to -- just to give you an example, to a number of individual things. A private trip with Milo Djukanovic, from Budve to Bar it stated that Milo Djukanovic -- that we had gone to Milo Djukanovic's house, whereas in fact Milo Djukanovic does not own a house there. I suggested a correction immediately. I never said that he had a house in Bar but that's what the transcript reflected. So there were a number of mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other material mistakes that you corrected at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had been part of this process for two and a half years. I can't remember what other errors there were, but there were other errors. Perhaps you may see fit to remind me. I can't remember now, but there were other mistakes and errors that I pointed out during my testimony in the Milosevic case. I certainly did not overlook them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to know is about these corrections. Were they inserted as you were testifying, or did you file a special written report containing these corrections with the investigators?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can no longer remember, after two years, whether I did this orally or in writing. At any rate, I made certain corrections. I made them clear to the Tribunal. This was a result of my misunderstanding, possible misunderstanding, with Mr. Williams and mistranslation. There were some other details which I deemed inessential. For example, the issue of weapons in Bar. I didn't know who was buying these weapons and who didn't. So there was discussion about this, whether it was Djukanovic or not. Anyway, I did make corrections back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your testimony, I was given these corrections in writing, a copy of these corrections that you suggested. What I want to know is: Before this, your new testimony in the Strugar case, did you go through your statement again with the OTP and point out these corrections that were handed to the Defence team in writing?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a few cursory marks about certain mistakes being there, which I believed were errors. The lady from the Prosecution told me that I should put this in writing, and I did, and this was to be submitted. There were some other small things, minute mistakes, which I did not believe were essential. But that was about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me an example? Can you tell me one of those small mistakes which you believe was incorrectly entered into your statement but does not truly make a difference?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several of those. On one of the pages, I had the Serbian version of the text. On the 7th of October, it says there was a meeting at the assembly, a debate of Lord Carrington's plan. This did not take place on the 7th, but rather on the 17th. So this must have been a typo. Or, for example, the way -- the song about the fairy wailing from the top of Lovcen, Dubrovnik forgive us, that song was mistranslated, in my opinion, but I didn't pay much attention to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But these are things that you consider minute, immaterial mistakes, which you did not pay any special attention to, like the one you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that I paid no attention to those. That's what you are claiming. I did pay attention, but I considered these mistakes to be not particularly significant, and I believe that those could be set right in the course of testimony and that other people could then recognise these mistakes. Lord Carrington's plan was not discussed on the 7th but on the 17th of October, because that's when he wrote it. That's clear enough. I don't think we should go any further into that, because it's quite clear that this debate took place on the 17th. I don't think it would make any sense for us to challenge that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony in answer to one of my questions, you said that you had undergone surgery due to health problems. Can you tell me when exactly this happened, the date and where, the place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just before I met the investigators, the OTP investigators, in Sydney, in the month of October, at a hospital in Sydney. Both my legs were amputated. My legs were amputated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said that already. But what I want to know is, is the date, if you remember, of the surgery itself.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several surgeries which took place throughout the month of September and October, just before the investigators arrived in Sydney.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we just make a little bit more specific, because when you say "September" and "October," this is not very specific. Can we have the exact dates, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had undergone seven or eight surgeries at that time, and I can't give you all the dates. I should go back to my documents and have a look to find out exactly when they were, if you really insist on knowing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can you tell us how long your rehabilitation was after these surgeries, roughly speaking, in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, post-operational or rehabilitation? What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean following surgery, how long did you have to stay in the hospital, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed for about ten days, five or six days, and then I was sent home, pursuant to a request that I made, following which investigators arrived from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was present when you gave the statement to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically, but there were several people. Mr. Williamson was there on behalf of the Court, Mr. Stefanovic, two people on behalf of the Australian authorities. That's four people. All together. The interpreter was there. I'd not used the services of this interpreter. And there was another person there. The driver too. Five or six people at my house, because this took place in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Two persons on behalf of the Australian authorities. Is one of them Darryl Parrish from the Australian federal police?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the gentleman's name. I assume that's correct, but you have them all listed on the front page, so you can check the names. I don't know their names by heart. The two gentlemen who had arrived on behalf of the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Darryl Parrish's name is on the front page, so what I want to know is if you know what the reason was for him attending this interview.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was probably there to see what was going on, because I am now an Australian citizen. I was granted Australian citizenship, and the Australian state probably wanted to know what was going on, what was happening to one of their citizens. I can't see any other reason for him being there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that on the last day of your interview, you signed the statement before the investigators, didn't you, or was that on a different day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on a different day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to move on to something else now. During your testimony, you said that you knew personally the former commander of the naval district, Kristo Djurovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell approximately how long you'd known that man for?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know their family. I know him. I know his sister. This is an honest family, a family of teachers, both their mother and their father are teachers. I've known them for a very long time. I can't tell you exactly how long, but it's an acquaintance of long-standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me for interrupting you, but let's not go too far into that. We can state, however, that you've known them for many years?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly, for quite many years [As interpreted]. His sister is married to Petar Kljakovic, a former schoolmate of mine, and we sailed together too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when Kristo Djurovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those first days, I think it was on 5th of October or thereabouts, that's when he was killed, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony you also stated that you knew Admiral Jokic while he was still in Boka Kotorska and before he became defence minister for Serbia. How long was that acquaintance?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't known him for very long. We met occasionally, but not too often. I was the manager of Jugooceanija and he was the commander of the military naval district, as far as I remember. So there were sporadic meetings. He would come to see me at my office, once, twice maybe. That was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what the cabinet was when he became the defence minister and who the Prime Minister was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He became a minister in the Serbian government. I think it was Zelenovic's government. But I can't tell precisely about his career and what he did in Belgrade. I know he was a minister with the Serbian government. Between his two stints in Boka Kotorska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the prime minister -- the president of Serbia at the time he was minister?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know personally any of the other high-ranking officers? And I'm referring to such ranks as general, admiral.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Nikola Tagovic [phoen], counter-admiral. I think that was the rank. He was also a schoolmate of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about General Jeremija and Damjanovic? Did you know them too?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know those generals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the period of time we are referring to, what were their exact positions?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly. I didn't know the ranks in the army precisely, but one of them was the commander of the Podgorica Corps, I believe, and the other was just a commander. They were highly positioned officers, high-ranking officers. I saw them at the meeting on the 1st of October, the presidency of Montenegro. I never met them after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell me more specifically, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What precisely?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Podgorica Corps, and what was the other man's position?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know they were highly positioned. They were high-ranking military officials, and that's why they attended the meeting that took place on the 1st of October. The meeting of the presidency and cabinet of Montenegro. It has, after all, been ten years since, and I am a sick man. It's very difficult for me to think back and remember correctly what their positions were. I know they were highly positioned military officers, but I don't know what positions specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 10, paragraph 4, it says that General Radomir Jeremija is the commander of the Uzice Corps and Radomir Damjanovic the commander of the Podgorica Corps. Can we use that to perhaps show that at the time you in fact knew their exact positions?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't say that I knew precisely even back then who was the commander of what. I knew they were high-ranking officers. I knew that they were in leading positions in the JNA, the army, that was allegedly defending the country. But that's all I can say, after 12 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 2000, was your memory perhaps fresher, since you were able to specify with a great degree of precision who held what position?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps this was the case, yes, but I don't think that even at the time I was perfectly certain about their respective positions, nor did I believe that to be particularly essential, who was the commander of which unit. I was not really interested, even at the time, in who commanded which specific unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you, but I think perhaps in that case you should not have provided such a specific answer, or you should have avoided specifying their positions, since Jeremija was at that time the commander of the Podgorica and not of the Uzice Corps, and Damjanovic was already part of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection. This is not examination; this is lecturing, and we'd ask, perhaps, if we could move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, you could put to the witness whether he would agree that each of the generals you've named held the positions you've identified. He will either be able to agree now or not. But for you to go on and say: "Well, you shouldn't have been more specific in your statement," is really comment rather than cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally know General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him personally. I only heard of him. I know who General Strugar was, but I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to General Strugar in person?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only talked to him via Jokic, and this is what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that. You never directly spoke to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did through Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question. I am asking you very precisely. I'm not asking you about Jokic. I'm asking you whether you spoke personally to General Strugar ever.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering. I spoke on the telephone with Jokic, who spoke with me on behalf of Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, who told me that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that they were talking to you on behalf of Strugar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic told me as follows: I and General Strugar --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, I have to interrupt you at this point. I need a very brief answer.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can you please warn the witness to answer my very brief and very precise questions, and I only need very brief and very precise answers from him. I believe my that question was very clear. The question was whether he ever spoke personally to Mr. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, the question is: Did you personally speak to General Strugar? Did you speak to the General himself or did you only speak through the Admiral? Can you tell us which it was, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke with General Strugar via Admiral Jokic. That's how I described it in my statement, and I stand by that. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We, I think, can accept that the General has not spoken personally -- that the witness has not spoken personally to the General, but spoke, he believed, to the general through Admiral Jokic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time you saw General Strugar, did you know what duties he discharged at the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw him, I also learnt what position he held. I've already told you that. You've already asked me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat: What was his position at the time when you saw him that evening and when you learnt about the position?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the operations group, and he was also the commander of the Territorial Defence of Montenegro. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, and I repeat: I was late coming to that session because I had a previous commitment. I went to Cetinje to escort Mr. Wejnaendts, deputy of Lord Carrington. When I returned, I found what I found as I've already described to you. My colleagues told me that General Strugar was there and they also told me what his position was and they also told me that the war had started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Did you hear of any other commander of any other operations group?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that evening. That's what I heard that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that before General Strugar, there was a Macedonian who was the commander of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was Uzunovski or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be General Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I didn't know him. I never saw him. I only heard of his existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear approximately when the former one was replaced by the latter?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not -- I wasn't there. I don't know when the change took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We could then deduce that Ruzinovski should have been the commander of the operations group before October, in any case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before October, most probably, before October, yes, certainly. I was informed that Strugar replaced this Macedonian, but not on the 1st of October, as you now insist. I'm sure that it must have been earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of any other general who discharged two sets of duties at the same time, who was in two positions in the army at the same time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember, but it would not have been unusual in the Yugoslav People's Army for somebody to occupy two or three positions at the time. That was a common practice in the Yugoslav People's Army from the end of the People's War during the Second World War and later on it did happen that one person would be in two or three positions at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Could you tell us: An operations group, what does it correspond to in the army? Would it be a brigade, a corps, an army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, it would correspond to an army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So General Strugar was at the same time the commander of the operations group, corresponding to an army, and the commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This should have been the case. Now, when he stopped being the commander of the Territorial Defence, I can't tell you. This is information that you can get from the army. I'm not aware of this information. The operations group approximately was something that Slobodan Milosevic later organised as the 1st, the 2nd, and the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Momir Bulatovic become president of Montenegro, the president of the presidency of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first multi-party parliamentary elections in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more precise about the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in December 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1990 and 1991, you resided in Montenegro. Do you know what kind of a military formation was stationed in Montenegro at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not interested in that. I was not interested in any military units in Montenegro that existed at that time. I know that there was the Podgorica Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Podgorica Corps, and at the sea?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the sea, there was the military naval district of Boka Kotorska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 14, paragraph 3 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. [Microphone not activated] If I may ask the Chamber to assist us in getting the English version of the statement, citation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English version, it is page 16, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "Since being appointed as president, Bulatovic always had regular meetings with the commander of the 2nd Army. Very often I would see higher-ranking officers of the JNA, usually generals, who arrived at these meetings with Bulatovic and Djukanovic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it possible, then, Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, how is something possible? I don't understand your question. What do you find impossible?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when Momir Bulatovic became president, you say that, in your written statement, that he always had regular meetings with the commander of the 2nd Army and that you would often see high-ranking officers of the JNA, usually generals, who arrived at these meetings with him. A little while ago, you said that at that time in Montenegro, there was only the Podgorica Corps stationed in Montenegro. There was no army. Can you please explain the discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain the discrepancy. You're quoting me about something that probably doesn't refer to the beginning of the war, but the time before the war. My office in Titograd was very close to Bulatovic's office, and I did see generals coming in and leaving. I didn't pay too much attention to that. And I didn't know whether he was the commander of the 2nd Army or the Podgorica Corps. At that time, I did not -- I was not interested in that. Maybe that is the explanation of this mistake. I do not find this very significant, whether a general is the commander of an army or the Podgorica Corps. As a civilian person, I didn't go into that and I didn't pay too much attention to that fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Please tell me: According to you, when did the war start?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Montenegro is concerned, it did not start before the 1st of October. In Yugoslavia, it started earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war started, which military formation was stationed in Montenegro? Was it a corps? Was it an army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly the Podgorica Corps, because Podgorica is the capital of Montenegro. There was the 5th Montenegrin in Titograd. That is the 5th Titograd Brigade, which was stationed in Masline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the war started, Montenegro did not have an army or a unit that would correspond to an army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Montenegro never had a unit corresponding to an army. I didn't say that Montenegro had a unit corresponding to an army. An army comprised much more than Montenegro ever had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come that President Bulatovic at that time had meetings with the commander of the 2nd Army, when there was no 2nd Army in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should not they be allowed to be in a meeting? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, there was no 2nd Army in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that there was the 2nd Army in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever it says, let it stay. This is the operations group. The army was created later on, when Yugoslavia was divided, when the organisation in the army was changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Counsel is misquoting from the English, and I can either bring it on redirect or just ask now that the Chamber be made aware of what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My understanding, Ms. Somers, is that the witness at the beginning indicated he did not really know what army groups were present. He did know that the Podgorica Corps was there, but otherwise, as a civilian, he took no interest. And the cross-examination has proceeded from that foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left Crna Gora in June 1992 up to the present day you say you have been following the situation in Montenegro via the Internet and via the media. Can you please tell me, if you remember, when Pavle Bulatovic was killed.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was approximately sometime in 1999. I can't tell exactly when. I know that he was killed in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to see whether you remember the time.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. It was either in 1999 or 2000, approximately. I don't know exactly. I can't remember exactly. I know that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Can you please tell me and explain how come that for the period between the summer 1990 to 16 February 1991, when you were discharging the duties of a member of parliament in the federal parliament, you didn't -- you were not aware of the decisions of the federal presidency from 1990 and 1991 about the illegal armament of paramilitary formations and the import of arms from Croatia, the order on disarmament, in the light of the fact that it was carried by all the media?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that there were a lot of contradictions about that. I did follow the media, and I can't tell you now, as I stand here today, what was going on. I have mentioned that there was a lot of controversy about that, and I believe that that was the case. How much weapons entered the state, I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow the situation with regard to Dubrovnik before the Tribunal in The Hague, in order to inform yourself who the accused was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the situation in Dubrovnik. Have you followed the situation? Did you inform yourself whether anybody was accused about what happened in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean whether I followed when I was at home in Australia? Yes, I did, as much as I could, as much as my health condition would allow me to follow all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who were the persons who were charged with the events that took place in Dubrovnik during the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that General Strugar was charged with those crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody else was charged?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there have been any other indictments. I know that there was an investigation for Momir Bulatovic. I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also hear that the Admiral Jokic was charged?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have reminded me of that. And Captain Kovacevic as well. I've heard that. I read it on the Internet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow the situation with General Jokic, what happened to him after the indictment was published?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read on the Internet that Admiral Jokic entered a guilty plea and pleaded guilty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Rules and the Statute of this Tribunal, or with the Dubrovnik indictment? I mean the full text. Because last time I saw you carrying a document, a hard-bound document, that exactly corresponds with the documents used here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you saw, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the document you were carrying.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the entire indictment on the Internet. It wasn't hard-bound or anything. I read it on the Internet, and anyone could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you referred to the Sava Kovacevic Brigade as an honourable, glorious name from the People's Liberation Struggle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that the Sava Kovacevic Brigade had taken part in military operations in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the Dubrovnik front; that's correct, the brigade. It wasn't called "brigade." I think you're twisting things around there. There are two distinct things. One is the 5th Montenegrin Brigade that was led by Savo Kovacevic. It is stationed in Podgorica. Another thing is a paramilitary unit called Savo Kovacevic. That was organised on the Dubrovnik front back in 1991, and then they set up two different units that were somehow associated with Savo Kovacevic, but those were two different things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 13, paragraph 2, in B/C/S, page 15, paragraph 1, you say that paramilitary units that were headed for Dubrovnik had soon gained a reputation. Several groups were openly referred to as Chetniks, and one of those units called itself the Sava Kovacevic unit. Further, on page 21 in the B/C/S version, in English it's page 25, paragraph 1, the sentence starts: "All those people cooperated closely with Novak Kilibarda, the head of the National Party, who had been at the forefront of setting up military formations. Velibor Voravic [phoen] from the Main Board of the party were sending volunteers to the existing groups and also established the Sava Kovacevic units." In the same paragraph, you refer to Zizic, Predrag Bulatovic, Novica Stanic, Predrag Popovic, as people who took part in organising paramilitary units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is what correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I've just read out of your statement.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The National Party took part in organising paramilitary units. It was one of the main factors in organising the attack on Dubrovnik on the part of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your opinion, the Sava Kovacevic Brigade, which took part in military operations was a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're insinuating again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please just tell me.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are insinuating. That's all I have to say. The 5th Montenegro Brigade is a regular JNA unit carrying on the traditions of the 5th Partizan Brigade from the liberation war and the Sava Kovacevic unit was organised in those days on the Dubrovnik front. Those were two different things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the rank of that paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Battalion, brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're calling it brigade, with no end in sight. I'm not sure where you get the idea at all. It was certainly a unit. It could have been a battalion, easily a brigade. I can't say. The main thing is that this paramilitary unit was set up to sling mud on the reputation of Sava Kovacevic and the People's Liberation struggle. That was their aim. How many people were involved, I can't say. The aim was to disgrace the JNA and Montenegro as well, Montenegro who cherished Sava Kovacevic as their greatest hero. The aim was not solely to conquer Dubrovnik and get as far as Karlobag. You're asking me. I'm answering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please stop shouting.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you're insinuating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have the Honourable Chamber here to stop me in case they believe I'm insinuating. They're keeping a watchful eye on this cross-examination, and they will be sure to intervene if necessary. So, in your opinion, we can completely rule out the possibility that the unit which went by the name of Sava Kovacevic was officially part of the Territorial Defence of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said this. Who said this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm drawing my own conclusions, because you said that a paramilitary unit that called itself Sava Kovacevic had been set up, which would seem to rule out the possibility that such a unit was in fact part of the regular forces of the Territorial Defence of Montenegro. It can't be both.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's your own conclusion, a conclusion that you have drawn. This was not my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain, then.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing for me to explain. I have told you about the existence of this unit. It was a paramilitary unit. It had been set up. Whether it was part of the TO or not, I can't say. That's not for me to say. How am I supposed to know that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me. There was a war. How the army is organised and what is being done at the time, I can't say with mathematical precision. To begin with, I was not fully aware of everything that was going on, and I never said I was. I only told you about things I knew. I never said otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you're stating. You're talking about things you know. You say that there was a paramilitary unit that called itself Sava Kovacevic. I'm going to try to phrase my question in a different way now. Was there a regular unit of the Montenegro Territorial Defence that called itself Sava Kovacevic and that also took part in military operations in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the Sava Kovacevic unit belonged to. Territorial Defence, was it merely a paramilitary unit, was it -- did it serve as some sort of camouflage for another Chetnik unit, I can't say. The priest Anfilohije was brought over to educate the army to traditional folklore music on the Dubrovnik front. Don't ask me who the unit belonged to. You should find someone else to ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that there were two units called Sava Kovacevic at the time in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but there were two units bearing the name of Sava Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me specifically, I'm asking you about 1991 and the Dubrovnik operation, the military operation. Were there two units at the same time that were called Sava Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you realise that people whom you referred to in Crna Gora, such as Predrag Popovic, have denied parts of your testimony, Novica Stanic, Zoran Zizic, said either you had been paid to lie or you just didn't know. All those people denied having taking part in the setting up of paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people you refer to are all members of the National Party, of course it's their right to claim they took no part. It is my position that they did take part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know this with sure and certain knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that what they did at the time was material to the entire process of organising paramilitary units, and they were in favour of taking Dubrovnik as quickly as possible, precisely the people you've now named.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, one would only expect them to deny these accusations, after so many years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you've ever been to Vinogradi Motel? Did you ever visit that place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go there in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your capacity as foreign minister for Montenegro's government, did you ever go to Vinogradi Motel?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those were things that journalists made up, and soldiers of the 7th Battalion, who claimed that I had gone there. I never even went to Herceg-Novi in those days. I never even got close. I can tell you this is a lie, nothing else. You shouldn't try too hard about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is a lie, an absolute lie?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was said the last time around, you're trying to say that I was in Vinogradi, whereas I wasn't. I know that things that have been pillaged the looted, the so-called war booty, was being collected there. That's what I learned about the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Zoran Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Kovacevic? Zoran Kovacevic? What do you mean? I think you're taunting me a little bit there. I never saw that man. Of course I heard about the man. I know that this man claimed to have met me and that I asked him to do some looting for me. That's nonsense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say you wanted from him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said in the papers, the Chetnik paper Dan - it's a broad sheet - that I had asked a man named Zoran Kovacevic to go and rob Tereza Kesovija's house and to bring for me a trailer from Dubrovnik. This is so low, so far below the belt that frankly I wonder why you're bringing this up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you publish any official denial of this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did. I said that this was nonsense. I never used a wheelchair in my life. As you see, I'm not using a wheelchair now. I was a sailor. Perhaps I would have asked him to steal a ship for me, or a yacht, but certainly not a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you're far off the mark, far off the mark. This doesn't make any sense at all. This is pure nonsense. I mean, I can't bring myself to believe that this is your level, that you should be insinuating things like these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not insinuating. I'm merely asking questions.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For God's sake. Yes, I see exactly the sort of questions you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever accused of embezzling $400,000 in Montenegro while you were the manager of Jugooceanija on or about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an allegation made by Slobodan Milosevic. This is also nonsense, the same kind of nonsense as the allegation that I had had Tereza Kesovija's house robbed. This is precisely the kind of thing that my testimony in the Milosevic case gave rise to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly on what days meetings of the Montenegro government or cabinet are held?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowadays I'm not aware of when exactly they take place, but in my time it was on Thursdays is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that JNA units had suffered losses on the very first day and that these losses were substantial. Do you know exactly what these losses, these casualties, were on the first day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I say that these losses had been substantial? Where did you read that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said during the examination-in-chief, in answer to a question by the OTP, and then you talked about how many people got killed, about 157 Montenegrins and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I found out from the official report that 157 Montenegros had been killed. I thought those were heavy losses, because Montenegro is a small country. I did keep an eye on how many people were getting killed, because as the manager of Jugooceanija, I was organising financial aid for the families of victims or the families of those who got killed. We provided financial assistance for mothers and widows. At that time, the count had already reached 100 in the first month. That's how it was at the time, roughly speaking. So those were the heavy losses that I spoke about, and those were indeed heavy losses, because Montenegro is a small country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, after you were shown the orders by Momir and Pavle Bulatovic, when he spoke about the kinds of weapons that were used on the Dubrovnik front, you go on to claim that the JNA units had suffered losses on the first day, that the losses were heavy, and you go on to say how many people got killed. Do you know this as a fact, that the JNA units suffered losses on the first day on the Dubrovnik front?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you're quoting me correctly. I know that the second or third day, coffins started arriving back, and that to the west of Dubrovnik, losses were greater than to the east, towards the Montenegro border. That's what I knew about, and that's the only thing I really spoke about. I didn't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened exactly, what the casualties were at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the west of Dubrovnik, in the direction of Ston and Trsteno [phoen], JNA units were being ambushed and people were killed. Those were the losses. Not all on the same day, of course, but every day TV covered these losses, these casualties, and brought the names of the people who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your work for the state authorities, did you ever attend a commemorative meeting or session held in honour of the victims who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. There were such meetings, but probably I did not attend, or maybe I was needed elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that such meetings were held, do you know when, on what specific occasion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd, perhaps, or perhaps on the 3rd of October, the 7th, in those days. There were meetings that were held, commemorative meetings that were held. I don't think I attended any of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Ivanica is?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Ivanica do you have in mind? There's one in Serbia and there's one near Trebinje, or rather, near Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose territory is that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a borderline town between Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It belongs to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I think it's a borderline town, but I can't say who it belongs to. Ivanica is -- straddles the road, the Dubrovnik-Trebinje road. I drove through many times, but I never really asked myself where it was officially in Herzegovina or Croatia. It used to be a single state, you know, so I took no interest in that, and I'm hardly able to determine that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that someone got killed in Ivanica on the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, no, I did not hear about anyone getting killed. The 1st of October, specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps later on you did hear about that, but what I'm asking is that: Did you hear that anyone was killed on the 1st of October in Ivanica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on that day, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the name of Nojko Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know who the person is?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I please have the usher's assistance. Your Honours, I would like to have copies of a newspaper article distributed that I will now show the witness. Then I will ask questions based on this newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I just make a point before we proceed? Because when counsel cross-examines and makes reference to the transcript, he has not been giving page numbers. I just wanted to indicate to the Chamber that the discussion about casualties appears on -- what I have is unofficial -- page 40 of the transcript of day 10. And I would be very grateful if the Chamber might instruct counsel to cite us to a place in the transcript. The reason I say that is it does not say what counsel said it says. It would be helpful to have it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Rodic, it would help the smooth conduct of the case if, when you're referring specifically to something in the transcript, if you were able to give a reference to it, it will make it easier for ourselves and for counsel for the Prosecution. Identify precisely what it is you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. This testimony so far has been very extensive. I've made notes. I've been using these notes while asking questions about what he has testified so far. In any case, if I need to resort to the transcript, I'll try and find the specific place in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are two texts. Actually, one article from the newspaper called Pobjeda.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is this from? Is this Pobjeda or is it not Pobjeda?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Pobjeda, dated 3 October, and the title is "The troops." Can you please read the framed part of this text, monitors and proves -- if you find it easier, I'll read it for you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that at the meeting in The Hague on Friday, it's going to be very hard. I'm mentioning a fact here --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. There's no indication of who authored this article, and that would be very helpful certainly to know whether this is an editorial or an article or just what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an article from the Pobjeda newspaper, as you can find it written on the margin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There's no attribution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems to be the case. I don't know that Mr. Rodic can do anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment, I can't, Your Honour. However, in any event, I believe that we can provide you with the original of the newspaper at a later stage, and I can deliver this original to the Honourable Chamber. This article, which was published on page 5 of the Pobjeda daily, dated 3 October 1991, the copy is somewhat illegible, because I received it via fax. However, the original, which I currently don't have on me, I can deliver to the Trial Chamber at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would simply object to any introduction into evidence until there's more of a predicate laid and identification of who wrote what, what the nature of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It can't be a basis for admission that the newspaper has not identified the journalist or editor that wrote a particular piece that it publishes. But the use that can be made of this at the moment would appear to me to be no more than to learn whether views attributed in the article to the witness, Mr. Samardzic, are his views or not, and I'm sure that's where Mr. Rodic is about to go. If they do not reflect the witness's views, that will be the end of these articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is precisely what I wanted to achieve with this article, because there are some parts which are emphasised under the title "monitors and evidence" referred to what the witness has said, as well as the part of the text entitled, "A commitment before The Hague conference." There's also a photo on this page depicting the session in commemoration of the fallen soldiers. I'm going to read this passage under the title "monitors and evidence." I quote: "I believe that it's going to be very hard at the meeting in The Hague on Friday. I am mentioning this fact because the international media who have organised themselves against us and yesterday in Dubrovnik monitors tried to prove that Dubrovnik had been attacked by the army and by Montenegrins. At the same time, our lads were dying in Herzegovina." This may be a language different to the one that we usually speak, but the objective is for us to prove that we have been attacked and that we are just doing our duty and defending our country. When it comes to the issue of Prevlaka, we have to prove that Prevlaka is part of our territory, the territory of Montenegro, and that it was never part of Croatia. What right do they have to claim this from us, to attack this? I see this as a huge tragedy and a huge misfortune. If things are as they are, we have to fight, we have to defend ourselves (Nikola Samardzic)."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, did you attend this session in commemoration of the fallen soldiers? Did you ever issue this statement? Did the journalists interpret you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I did not attend this session. I'm not in this photo. I'm not there. Secondly, I didn't give a statement like this. I did speak at one of these sessions, saying that we were getting ready for a war, but this is not what I said. I have to remind you, Mr. Rodic, that this is Pobjeda, and Pobjeda was edited by an ultranationalist who wrote all sorts of things those days, and he set the tone and he put words into people's mouths that they never said themselves. So at that time it was a disgrace. Pobjeda was a disgraceful daily. Allow me to finish this. If you look at -- please allow me. You've asked me a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, would you please pause. Could I ask you whether these words reflect what you said in any public statement or to a journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that on the 1st of October, when I'd heard that we were attacked, I said that we would defend ourselves. This is the only I think that I said. I've already said that. And if there is anything else that I said in public, it was about the way we should behave in The Hague at the peace conference. I couldn't say where people were killed, when people were killed, because I didn't know that. I wasn't aware of that. At that time, the media brought all sorts of lies that referred to war operations and to my engagement in Jugooceanija. This is a really long story. I wouldn't go into that. One of the things that were carried at the time was that I embezzled money. But I was attacked by that daily because of my political views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, you're going beyond my question. If you'd just pause there. You have indicated that the comments at the very last part of the first article, which is dealing with monitors and evidence, on page 4, is it, reflects something that you did say. Did you speak in public about Prevlaka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. On several occasions I spoke publicly about Prevlaka. But I never said that Prevlaka belonged to Montenegro. I said that Prevlaka was Croatian territory that we had to gain, that we had to get. I had transcripts of the session of the parliament of Montenegro, and I said that we had to gain Prevlaka in negotiations. That was my position. I said that we could get Prevlaka only if we negotiated with Croatia rather than if we waged a war against Croatia. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that what is recorded here in this newspaper article does not reflect what you have said publicly or to a journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very often I spoke about Prevlaka on TV and in papers. My position is very clear on Prevlaka. I have a lot of documents about that, Your Honour. I did say that we had to get Prevlaka, but that Prevlaka was Croatian and that we could only get Prevlaka if we negotiated with Croatia. And in that respect, I also have a book by Hrvoje Kacic, in which it says that Bulatovic and I negotiated with President Tudjman about Prevlaka. We had a special meeting in The Hague. We did not inform Milosevic about this meeting, and we said at that time to President Tudjman that Prevlaka was Croatian but that Montenegrins had to have it because it closed the entrance into the Boka Kotorska bay and that it naturally belonged to Montenegro but that we had to make that official through negotiations. It was our position -- and not only mine, but the position of the Montenegrin authorities to negotiate, and that was our initiative. Everything else is a blatant lie and trying to set me up. We started the initiative to negotiate the issue of Prevlaka and ended the war in that way. The facts are totally different than what Mr. Rodic is now trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic isn't trying to say anything, Mr. Samardzic, nor am I trying to say anything. I am trying to find out whether what is written in this article reflects what you have said or contradicts or is different from what you have said, and it is very difficult to understand what your answer is, because you don't answer that question. Because you don't answer that question. You go on to give a long speech about your views on the subject instead of saying: "Yes, I said this," or "No, I did not say this." If you can understand that both. Rodic and I simply want to know whether you said what is here or whether you didn't. That's all we need to know at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Rodic, does that help you at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am trying to get at that myself, and I would for that like to thank you. I'm just going to follow up on your last question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, can you tell me: Pobjeda, whose paper was that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the public paper of the Assembly of Montenegro at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The editor in chief that you've mentioned, Konatar, was he appointed by the Assembly of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you have just said that you did not say this, did you issue an official denial?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were attacks against me from all sides. I did not try to deny anything. There was no way for me to deny so many words used against me at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me when this was, what year, what date, and who attacked you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were constant attacks during that period. Some of them were because of Jugooceanija. The others were about my political positions, about the war in Dubrovnik, and Pobjeda the attacks were the strongest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any articles which showed these attacks or demonstrated these attacks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do they date from, let's say, October 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of articles attacking me in Pobjeda. If you want me to furnish you with these, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So it would be true to say that this part of the article that we have just read was made up by the editor in chief or one of the journalists, and you never said that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody just twisted my words around in order to adapt it to the then prevailing policies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you read the part entitled, "Commitments before The Hague conference," from the top to the first paragraph under the photo?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. However, I believe that this is just one of the positions that they brought at the time about The Hague conference. I didn't pay much attention to that, because they wrote what they wanted to write, as they pleased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the units of MUP, of the Republic of Croatia, attack the units of JNA in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and did the reservists and soldiers serving in the JNA who were from Montenegro die in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that something like that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak about this event? Did you issue any positions on this event?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't issue any positions on this event. I was aware of the fact that soldiers were killed beyond the territory of Dubrovnik municipality and that these soldiers were from Montenegro. I was a civilian. I did not therefore issue any particular statements on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you not worried by the fact that soldiers who were members of the JNA and who hailed from Montenegro were getting killed in Bosnia-Herzegovina by Croatian units?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I was greatly concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it not have been a natural thing for you, as a minister, to do to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. But look at the way you're phrasing your questions. I did speak about that, but that was not the only theatre of war at the time. It wasn't only in Bosnia; it was also in Dubrovnik. It was around Cilipi. It was in Konavle. So probably at one point it spread to Herzegovina because it's very close to the border. So it spread to Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not issue any official comments, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No particular comments. I held talks about Prevlaka. I spoke about The Hague conference, and those were my reports to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I am keeping track of the time, but if I may just finish this question concerning this different section from the same article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here you have a caption saying, "Commitments before The Hague conference." It reads: "Nikola Samardzic, foreign minister, in his report, expressed his views regarding the expectations from The Hague conference. Speaking about the conference, Samardzic reminded those present that Montenegro's delegation had taken a flexible attitude to the Yugoslav crisis in order to find a solution and cease hostilities. However, developments near the Croatian border, and especially developments between Ravno and Slano clearly show that the losses suffered by our units were to a very high extent suffered in a territory that does not belong to Croatia but rather to Bosnia and Herzegovina, that MUP units arrived and ambushed our own units, all of which clearly indicates that Montenegro has been attacked by the Croatian MUP with intent. This is an attack on the JNA. This is an attack on young Montenegrins who are serving in the JNA. I said this to the Croatian side openly -- to the Serbian side openly that our boys were better than those from Valjevo." Did you indeed state this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say this, but I think these were reports that relate to the period before the 1st of October. On the 16th of September, Momir Knezevic and I travelled to The Hague to attend the conference of foreign ministers, the peace conference, and at the conference I spoke about the incidents in Herzegovina and about our people being killed there. That's what I spoke about. But this related to the period before the 3rd of October and before the 1st of October, but rather, in September, before war operations began. That's when Momir Knezevic and I went to The Hague and that's when I spoke about some of the things that you have referred to. I clashed with Minister Separovic, the Croatian minister, because my position was that our units were being attacked from churches, and that's the discussion that we had, and that's the discussion that you're probably referring to. But this has nothing to do with the 3rd of October or with battles during the Dubrovnik operation. This was before the operation even began. Secondly, Ravno is not on Montenegro's side of the border to Croatia. It's on the other side, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just ask you the following: When you say that you made protestations to the Croatian minister, Separovic, in relation to attacks against our lads, or our people, can you tell us who specifically you mean? Who was attacked in Bosnian territory?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day I travelled with Momo Knezevic, I learned that our lads had been killed in Herzegovina, and I spoke about that. I spoke to Lord Carrington about that. Of course I defended Montenegro. What else was I supposed to do? Separovic was angry with me for saying that, and a debate ensued. That was in mid-September, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mid-September. Did you have any reliable or more precise information about the Croats opening fire on those units, JNA units, from churches and religious buildings? Do you know what specifically these buildings and churches were?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any longer. I know that I was told that fire was being opened from churches and religious facilities, and that some of our lads had been killed. I spoke about that at the meeting, and I told Separovic about that. Separovic was mad. He said that I was attacking the Croatian churches. I said at the time: "If you open fire from a religious building, it ceases to be a religious building; it becomes a firing position." That was my attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this may be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just an administrative matter from the transcript. If I could just let the transcriber know on page 30, line 23, there is a line of questioning that is attributed to me but it in fact is Mr. Rodic's, and it would be helpful, I think, just to clear that up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, have you finished your questions on this newspaper particle?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you wanting it marked for identification, or are you not wanting to pursue it at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I do want it marked for identification, Your Honour. We shall at a later stage provide you with the original copy, as I promised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, what we have at the moment, the document that is being shown to Mr. Samardzic and which he has spoken about, will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D16 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's marked for identification as D16, Mr. Rodic. Now, do we correctly understand that you must be drawing near the end of your cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid I can't confirm this. I hope you will understand that this is a very important witness, both to the Defence and to the OTP, and I believe you have seen the kind of problem that I'm facing during my cross-examination. I must point out that when my learned friend and colleague Ms. Somers examined this witness about everything that had to do with Montenegro or the JNA, there was no section of the answer saying: "Yes, but at the same time the Croats were doing this or that, or the Croatian army were doing this or that." Whatever I asked in relation to Croatia regularly I got an answer which had more to do with the Serbs and Montenegrins. I was not even able to interrupt the witness to avoid unnecessary conflict. Therefore, I was forced to spend the best part of my cross-examination dealing with answers that were unduly long and off the mark. Therefore, I believe that I could finish my cross-examination in the course of the next session after the break. I hope that Your Honours will understand my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I know we all have a desperate need for a break, but I must say that if in fact I would put a standing objection to relevance if the issue is going to be what did the Croatians to, what did the Croatians do, to colloquially, as it is referred to in this Tribunal, is in no way relevant to what was done by the side that is represented by General Strugar's presence here, and I would simply ask the Chamber to assist us in making sure that we don't have to get up with considerable standing objections to relevance, if that is going to be the continued ground of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will deal with those matters if and as they arise, Ms. Somers. Your cross-examination has gone on for considerable time, Mr. Rodic. We are conscious of the difficulties you have experienced at times, and for that reason we've allowed you to carry on this long, but we look forward to your cross-examination concluding during the next session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I'll do my best to comply with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, on page 14 of the English version, paragraph 4 -- paragraph 2, you say: "When the next session -- when the next government meeting was held on the 4th of October, I was already strongly opposed to war." On the same page, in paragraph 3 of the English version of your statement, you say: "However, at the session held on the 4th of October, I expressed my strong opposition to war. No one, however, was much bothered by what I had to say, because in their eyes, everything was going smoothly." Is it true that you said this at a government meeting, at a cabinet meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said this at the cabinet meeting. I said that I believed this war was unnecessary and that we should not fight in Dubrovnik. It was on the 4th or 7th of October. It was on either of these two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is the records of a meeting of the Montenegro government. We have made copies of the first two pages, the front page and the next page, where you can see who was in attendance at the meeting. In the further course of our examination, if necessary, we shall provide the full minutes, the full minutes, however, are quite extensive. Mr. Samardzic, the document you have in front of you is the minutes from the 46th meeting of the Montenegro government, held on the 26th of September, 1991. The next thing you have is the minutes of the 47th government meeting, held on the 3rd of October, 1991. The third thing is the minutes of the 48th government meeting of the Republic of Montenegro, held on the 10th of October, 1991. Let us, please, start with the last one, the one that took place on the 10th of October, on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. These are not minutes per se. This is simply records of attendance and the first page of a document called "Minutes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was made clear, as I understand it, by Mr. Rodic, that he, for the moment, merely was offering to the witness the first page of much more extensive minutes. Do you have any objection on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
