utterances.text: As long as the record reflects that what is being shown is only the first page, and if in fact it comes to pass that we need to have the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Rodic has foreshadowed that, if necessary, that will be made available. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last document, dated 10th of October. Absent from the meeting are Nikola Samardzic, Pavle Bulatovic, and Predrag Obradovic. You can see that you were absent from that meeting, can't you? It's in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was the manager of Jugooceanija and foreign minister. I did not attend all these meetings right from the start, nor did I reside in Podgorica. I drove over from Kotor and I would usually make it to the meeting halfway through the meeting or towards the end, late in the meeting. So these minutes that you are showing me, Mr. Rodic, were -- these notes were made at the beginning of the meeting. I am sure that I did not attend the beginning of this meeting. However, at some point in the course of the meeting, I would arrive and I would take part in its work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you arrive at the session on the 10th of October?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically, but I know that I came to all these meetings. Well, there were meetings that I couldn't attend, meetings that I was absent from, but as a rule, on account of my dual position, I would usually make it halfway through the meeting for the simple reason that I did not reside in Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The government meeting dated the 3rd of October, again it says absent, Zoran Zizic, vice-president of the government, Predrag Obradovic, Vojin Djukanovic, Pavle Bulatovic, and Ilija Lakusic and Nikola Samardzic, members of the government. Did you attend that meeting on the 3rd of October?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably arrived halfway through the meeting. I was late, as usual. As I said, I would usually arrive halfway through the meeting, on account of my dual position, and I would drive from Kotor to Podgorica for these meetings, because I did not live in Podgorica. And that's why these minutes reflect what they do. I was not there as a rule at the beginning but I would arrive halfway through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your statement that you attended these cabinet meetings, even if you were not there for the beginning of each single meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the meetings, yes. It's been a very long time and I can't remember specifically which I attended and which I didn't. On some days, I may have been absent, because I had been away on business. However, I did attend some of the meetings and some others I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you there on the 3rd?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think I arrived halfway through the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure or is this merely an assumption?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that I was there on the 3rd and on the 7th. I arrived from Kotor and I attended part of the cabinet meeting, after which I would drive back to Kotor. That was my regular routine concerning my work for the government at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The minutes dated 26th of September, 46th meeting of the government, Jusuf Fetahovic, Nevica [phoen] Avramovic and Nikola Samardzic are listed as absent. Did you also attend this meeting, the 26th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not, because as far as I can remember, I was away at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These seven-day intervals between the meetings, the 26th of September, the 3rd of October, and the 10th of October, what about those?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an extraordinary situation, and the government convened meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These specific documents we're looking at, do these correspond with the weekly meetings of the government?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in their entirety. The 3rd and the 7th, for example, there's no seven days in between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 3rd and the 10th?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 3rd and 10th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 26th of September and the 3rd of October, does that correspond?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This means that the 4th of October and the 1st of October sessions of the government are not here. These minutes are missing, the meetings that you've referred to in the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender these minutes into evidence and to be marked for evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first page of what is tendered as the minutes of the 46th, 47th, and 48th sessions of the government of Montenegro will be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D17.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that there were attacks on the JNA barracks in Prevlaka and also on other military facilities? That was in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. There could not have been an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the barracks, to the military facility, the JNA barracks in Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no barracks in Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, in Prevlaka, there were the buildings that now exist did not exist. It was a military barracks, not barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were there attacks by the Croatian forces on the military base?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about the problems of blocking roads, attacks on military facilities and persons in the territory of Dubrovnik municipality and in Herzegovina by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about the problems in connection with the blocking of the roads, attacks on military facilities and persons, in the territory -- in the general area of Dubrovnik and Herzegovina, carried out by the Croatian forces, the MUP and the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that obstacles were placed on the roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about attacks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I just heard that there were obstacles on the roads, that roads were being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Ludvig Pavlovic is? Did you hear of that name ever? Let me remind you. Radusa 1972.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ludvig Pavlovic, no. No. What happened in 1972, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, in the evening hours, the chief of the security centres of Montenegro, Ivan Jovanovic, distributed a paper according to which Croats were involved in incidents around Dzermin [phoen], and you said this was not a war threat. Can you please be more specific as to what it said on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a report issued by the security centre from Herceg-Novi. According to this report, there were a few incidents on the border with Croatia. Amongst other things, there was also an exchange of fire around the village of Zvinje [phoen] and that had happened a few days before that. In any case, he drafted a list of all these discords, that is, incidents, which happened on the border with Croatia, which is not long. It goes from Siroki Brijeg [As interpreted] to Prevlaka. This report did not show that the war had begun. It just showed that there was some discords and some difficulties in communication on border crossings between Croatia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be more specific: Did you hear from this Jovanovic [As interpreted] or from anybody else, about a report or some information which pointed to the fact that the Croatian forces had opened fire on the territory of Montenegro in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivanovic [As interpreted] didn't say at the time that fire was opened on the territory of Montenegro. It was Herceg-Novi radio that claimed that there was cannon fire opened by Croatia on the territory of Montenegro. I don't believe this to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Can we ask for a clarification? Because we believe we heard something in B/C/S and that it came out differently on the transcript. And that would be on page 47, line 22 and 23, where Mr. Rodic asked about something, and the answer was: "It goes from Siroki Brijeg to Prevlaka." We thought we heard a different answer about -- something Brijeg, and I wondered if that could be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 48, line 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No. 47 -- excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So is that correct? I just wanted to know if that stands. It's difficult, because we believe we heard something differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll wait to see if it's possible to get an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I believe I can clarify what Ms. Somers is referring to, page 47, line 22. It says, "Siroki Brijeg," and I believe that we will all agree, including Mr. Samardzic, that he said Debeli Brijeg. From Debeli Brijeg to Prevlaka, not from Siroki Brijeg to Prevlaka. And I believe that this is what Mr. Samardzic says, and I believe that this is what Ms. Somers is referring to. That's number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That does help us enormously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second thing which is also wrong, that's page 48, line 5, it says: "Herzegovina radio," and Mr. Samardzic said: "Herceg-Novi radio," not Herzegovina radio, but Herceg-Novi radio. So can this also be taken into account, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. There seems to be general agreement that those two names may have been wrongly recorded in the first place, and we will ask the interpretation and transcript people to check those matters with that clarification from Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 12, paragraph 4 of your statement in English, you said that in Dubrovnik there were just a few not heavily armed young men, and that was the only defence that the town had. On page 16, paragraph 1, you say Croats practically did not have any defence forces, and what they did have, they pulled out and used to defend the city of Dubrovnik. On your examination-in-chief, you mentioned that your friend, Hrvoje Kacic, a high Croatian official, and that his son, who was in the position not to go into the army, decided not to do that, but he instead decided to defend Dubrovnik. Can you then tell me: How come so many JNA soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, there were no Croatian troops in Dubrovnik. During the operations in Dubrovnik, a lot of Croats came to help the Dubrovnik defence, and they organised themselves and defended the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What forces arrived? What troops arrived, where from, and when?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you any detail on how the Croatian command brought the troops into Dubrovnik and how they defended the town. I only know that at the beginning there were no Croatian troops in Dubrovnik. There were just a few Croatian soldiers. And during the operations around Dubrovnik, the Croatian army grew in numbers and they defended the town. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say at the beginning there were very few troops or defenders of Dubrovnik, do you know that for a fact or do you just assume that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Dubrovnik, and I didn't count them. But in any case, it was clear that there were no big troops in Dubrovnik at the beginning of operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is your assumption, then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not just my assumption. It was obvious from the reports which were sent from the front line, which were aired, not only on Montenegrin TV, but also on CNN and on SkyNews. It was obvious that there were no large troops there but that gradually defence was being stepped up and that the town was being defended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Croatian forces, MUP and the ZNG, outside of the city walls and in the general area of Dubrovnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were defence forces of Dubrovnik in the territory of what we call Dubrovnik municipality. The municipality of Dubrovnik overlaps with the former Dubrovnik republic, and during the Dubrovnik operations, the number of troops that defended the town increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be more precise: From the 1st October in Ivanica, eight soldiers died in mortar fire. Who opened that fire?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they were killed. I only heard that. On the 1st of October, there was a session at which nobody spoke about those fallen soldiers. It was either on the 2nd or on the 3rd, or one of the following days, but not on the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to you, if this is on the 2nd or on the 3rd October --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of those days, or even later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have it that way. However, if they died from a mortar shell on either the 2nd or the 3rd of October in Ivanica, which is in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, how do you explain that? How do you account for that? Where were the Croatian forces at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the territory of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the territory of Dubrovnik? Do you only mean the town or the general area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the general area. Somebody must have opened fire from the territory of Konavle, towards Ivanica, and the shell probably crossed the border of the municipality of Dubrovnik. It went all the way to the municipality of Trebinje and killed some people. This is not impossible. And this is more or less what happened. Croats opened fire on a JNA unit and the guys were killed. I believe that that was the case. I was not there, but I know that on the 2nd or on the 3rd, our lads did die, and it was reported on TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any case, they killed from the Croatian fire?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already confirmed that. 157 Montenegrins died during the Dubrovnik operations that lasted over a period of several months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can agree then that we are not talking about just a few troops with very few weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that these 157 didn't die at the beginning, on the first or second day. That 157 lads died throughout the entire Dubrovnik operation. During that operation, Dubrovnik stepped up its defence gradually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that during the first three days, 15 members of the JNA were killed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some were killed. I'm not aware of the fact that 15 died. They reported some numbers on TV. I don't think it was 15, but I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number of the guys who were killed during the first couple of days. But in any case --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can give you their names, and I can assure that 15 JNA soldiers during the first couple of days [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However many died during these first days, as director of Jugooceanija, I would send out people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Hrvoje Kacic's son went to Dubrovnik to defend it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly, but I know that he went there immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he volunteer or was he a member of a military unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that he was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your examination-in-chief, you mentioned the visit of several foreign ambassadors who wanted to talk to General Strugar and who wanted to visit the Dubrovnik front line in the theatre of war in October 1991. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some ambassadors. I was supposed to attend this meeting with the ambassadors, and I didn't want to participate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in contact with the ambassadors on behalf of the military?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come it was him who attended the meeting with the ambassadors? How come he received them?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection. Speculation. How would he know? How would he know how -- why Admiral Jokic received them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will see whether the witness can offer an explanation. I suspect that you are correct, but we'll see what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was it who appointed Admiral Jokic to attend this meeting with the ambassadors, but I know that Admiral Jokic held several meetings with them. He even took a boat to Tivat. But he wouldn't allow them to go to the Dubrovnik theatre of war. They wanted to go and see Konavle. Mr. Hall [phoen], the British ambassador, and some other ambassadors from Western European countries, and the deputy ambassador of the United States. They all tried to enter the war area around Dubrovnik. But they couldn't do that. Together with Admiral Jokic, they went to Tivat in Herceg-Novi instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these ambassadors arrived, did you get in touch with Jokic? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't get in touch with him. I didn't go to any of these meetings. I believe that Momir Bulatovic told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not important. I'm trying to follow up on this. You said that you knew that Jokic wouldn't take them to the front line, that he took them from Tivat to Herceg-Novi and back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew he wouldn't take them to the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that they didn't go anywhere, and this was confirmed to you by your friend Hrvoje Kacic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Hrvoje Kacic told me that he was not satisfied with the treatment that Jokic accorded to these ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Do you know that as ambassadors on that occasion went to Dubrovnik and that they drafted a detailed written report covering their visit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was on a different occasion when they were at Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about this occasion.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this occasion they didn't go to Dubrovnik. They went to Dubrovnik on a different occasion. Allow me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then tell us exactly what these two occasions were? Can you be very precise?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ambassadors were in Dubrovnik at the beginning of November and this first occasion was in October. The ambassadors arrived on several occasions. On several occasions they tried to enter the theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When in October?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I believe it was the 25th of October or one of these dates. That was when the first meeting was in Tivat and in Herceg-Novi and on that occasion they didn't enter Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we are talking about the time around the 25th October?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I don't know any details after 15 years. I can't give you the exact date when it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, could you just pause a little? The translation is under pressure. They've caught up now, but if you could just slow the pace.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Rodic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm saying is what I said a moment ago. In October, the ambassadors drew up a detailed, written report on their visit to Dubrovnik, and it is my submission that your friend Hrvoje Kacic misinformed you on that occasion, because there is a written report and the OTP have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is testimony. This is not examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's ambiguous whether it's being put as a statement or put as a question. I'm sorry, Ms. Somers. Do you understand the point of objection, Mr. Rodic? Will you make clear which way you're going. If you've got a question, put it, but don't be asserting facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that your friend Hrvoje Kacic misinformed you deliberately regarding the ambassadors' -- the foreign ambassadors' visit to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that he did not misinform me. I am telling you: These are two different events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now, please, go back to your statement as it relates to the meeting that took place on the 1st of October, which we have already spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, during the break, I checked my previous submission from our last hearing, to the effect that during his testimony in the Milosevic case, Mr. Samardzic categorically did not correct his statement about the cabinet meeting on the 1st of October in Montenegro and Admiral Jokic being there. I have a copy of the relevant portion of the transcript from that testimony, where this same witness, in answer to a question by the Prosecutor, Geoffrey Nice, speaks about the meeting without pointing out that Admiral Jokic was not present at the meeting. So there was no kind of correction whatsoever. Can I have the usher's assistance, please. This is from the 8th and 10th of October, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You offer these as extracts from the transcript of the trial of Mr. Milosevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. The transcript is dated the 8th of October, 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, can you please go through this and tell me if you see any references by yourself to Admiral Jokic, or any corrections being made as to the fact that Admiral Jokic did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reference to Admiral Jokic's attendance or non-attendance here. However, during my testimony in the Milosevic case, if I remember correctly, I said clearly that he was not there. I should, however, go through the whole transcript to be able to say with any degree of certainty. If you only look at this page, you can't tell. However, if you go through the entire transcript, I believe you will find a reference to that. I believe you will find that I said that Jokic was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps Ms. Somers can help us with this, because she promised to go through the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection. First of all, there is a question. This is re-direct examination. I'm working from a different paginated number. I'm working from the first edition of the transcript. But if Mr. Rodic is going to use this, it would be very helpful, in my assertion, that he actually asks what question was asked and then what answer was given, and that all references that are contained in that answer are properly sourced back to the other references in the transcript. This is a very misleading point of cross-examination, and I will certainly explore it and attempt to clarify it on redirect, but right now you're getting -- I submit the Chamber is getting a very inappropriate view of what actually took place in that courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is offered at the moment, Ms. Somers, is two extracts from the transcript of the 8th of October, pages 11185 and 11186. The witness agrees that in those extracts, he makes no mention that Admiral Jokic was not there. Mr. Rodic has asserted from the counsel table that this is the -- that there is no reference anywhere in the transcript. The witness says he is sure that he did, but he would need to correct the whole transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And read the whole transcript. I believe if the matter is left there, the foundation is laid for your re-examination, in which, if there is a very different picture, you will be able to present it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will do that. Thank you. Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to make sure that the Chamber realised that the question itself was not presented to the Chamber, only the answer, and the question is very relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I made an effort to extract the relevant question from the Milosevic transcript, as related to the 1st of October meeting and who was present. As I promised, I did go through the entire transcript, and there's not a single reference or any correction as concerns the presence or absence of Admiral Jokic at the meeting on the 1st of October, 1991. Along the same lines, on behalf of the Defence, I can offer the entire transcript of this witness in the Milosevic case. I believe, however, that this would unduly encumber the transcript. Should you, nevertheless, so require, I am ready to offer the entire transcript into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We ourselves would not require the entire transcript. Ms. Somers has indicated that she will, in re-examination, be returning to this subject. The second point made by Ms. Somers is something you may be able to deal with, though. She points out that you do not at the beginning of this extract, you have not identified the question that is being answered. And it is Ms. Somers's submission that that question affects or may affect the answer that was given. So if you want to include the question at this point, that could be helpful to the Chamber. Otherwise, I'm sure Ms. Somers will do so when she comes to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is in line 16 on page 11185. The question is: "Who was there? What were they talking about?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that is perhaps enough to deal with that point of Ms. Somers' concern. As I've indicated, we do not require the whole transcript from that trial to be tendered to us. Do you want this to be marked for identification, this extract?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive the extract from pages 11185 and 11186 as being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D18.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the witness confirmed upon questioning that he knew Admiral Jokic well, in the sense of knowing him personally, and that they go back to before 1991, while the Admiral was the commander of the navy, or rather, the naval district in Boka, I must again ask you the following question, Mr. Samardzic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you make seven references to Admiral Jokic in your statement, in different parts of your statement, as attending this particular meeting, and even speaking at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I never said that I knew him well. I said that I'd met him two or three times before the war, while he was serving in Boka Kotorska. That's what I said. Secondly, I did not make seven references to him attending the meeting. I didn't exactly count all the references, but if count we must, then let us count. Can you please allow me to finish this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I may have made a mistake. It was half dark, or night. I made a mistake. I corrected that mistake, and it was never my intention to accuse Admiral Jokic of anything that he did not do or to assert that he was present when in fact he wasn't. I made a mistake that I later corrected, and that's all I can tell you in this respect. The mistake was not deliberate. How it came about, I can't say right now. It was after I had undergone major surgery. I was sick. I said that in my statement. But I did not mean harm. I made a reference to Jokic, and it entered the transcript and stayed there. It's an error.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This is what I have on your corrections, what I got from the OTP. These corrections are to be made, as indicated by the witness, immediately before your testimony, under item 4: Admiral Jokic was not present at the extraordinary meeting of the government on the 1st of October, 1991. And item 5: The witness believes that Kristo Djurovic had probably been killed. What was said in connection with Jokic's presence at the meeting should be ignored. These are the corrections you requested immediately prior to your testimony here in the Strugar case. The reference is page 12, paragraph 3 -- my apologies. Page 12, paragraph 1, as indicated by the OTP, the English version page 10, paragraph 4, and page 11, paragraph 6. However, in addition to these two corrections on page 12, paragraph 3 of the English statement, when you say that Strugar said it was a fortunate circumstance that the Montenegrins would fight and the JNA would defend Yugoslavia from aggression, that Dubrovnik would be liberated from the Ustasha at a minimum cost. There were plenty of Ustasha there so the army would have to proceed with caution, he said. You say that Jeremija, Damjanovic, Jokic, and especially Babic echoed his statement, especially Babic, who spoke a lot at the meeting. You never corrected this. Allegedly, these words were uttered by General Strugar and repeated by Admiral Jokic, which would seem to imply that he spoke at the meeting. However, this has never been corrected. Please, don't try to interrupt me. Do you have an answer to this, in connection with the corrections, I've read out the two corrections that you made, but you made no corrections regarding this.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just read, everything that has to do with Admiral Jokic's presence has been corrected. My correction relates to the entire portion of the statement as the statement relates to Admiral Jokic. Therefore, it's been corrected. Perhaps you're now telling me that this specific remark was not corrected, has not been corrected. But as you said yourself a while ago, everything that relates to Admiral Jokic should be ignored. That's what the correction said. So that's precisely how it should be read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your attention drawn by the OTP to the fact that you were to exclude Admiral Jokic from this alleged meeting that took place, allegedly, on the 1st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me anything in relation to that. I said myself right at the start in my testimony in the Milosevic case. I realised that an error had been made, and I was very sorry about that. It has been perpetuated in the transcript, and there's nothing I can do about it at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it still your submission that you corrected this statement during your testimony in the Milosevic case and clearly stated that the Admiral was not present?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been two or three years since, and I believe that I did state that. I was having an argument with Milosevic, and in the course of this argument, I can't be a hundred per cent certain about this, however, I did say that Admiral Jokic was not there. You keep insisting on this, but your claim about the seven references is certainly not accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's all right, then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further, in relation to this story about the 30.000 Ustashe, let me point this out to you again. On page 10, paragraph 5, when you speak about the cabinet meeting on the 1st of October, you said that Djukanovic presided over the meeting and Bulatovic was present too. Bulatovic spoke about 30.000 Ustashe having attacked Montenegro and that we had to put up a fight. Throughout your statement, the name of Momir Bulatovic was only mentioned in connection with the making public of this number, 30.000 Ustashe. All other references, all additional references to civilian or military personnel, you never link them up with this particular claim about the 30.000 Ustashe. For the very first time in your testimony in the Milosevic case, on page 11186 of the transcript, line 6, you say that Bulatovic said the thing about 30.000 Ustashe and that this had been made known by General Strugar. This is your first reference to General Strugar in connection with Bulatovic's statement, whereas here, in this case, during the examination-in-chief, and when cross-examined by myself, you said that when you joined the meeting, the meeting that was already under way, the first time you heard this was when General Strugar spoke about the 30.000 Ustashe advancing on Montenegro. Can you please explain how your statement in 2000 and in the Milosevic case, where you added the name of General Strugar after that of Momir Bulatovic, and now, testifying in the Strugar case, how did this come about that suddenly you claim that General Strugar was the first person whom you heard talk about this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no discrepancy there. I'll say this again. When I came to the meeting, the meeting was halfway through, or maybe even into the second half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know that. But can you explain these obvious discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any obvious discrepancies there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That's an answer too. That's an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. This is another excerpt from the transcript of the testimony of this witness in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 11433, on re-examination by the Prosecution, line 5, to Mr. Geoffrey Nice's question as to what the approach of General Strugar to this meeting was, the witness answered: "I heard Strugar, and he confirmed -- I heard Strugar confirm Bulatovic." Again, this means that Bulatovic said this, and then General Strugar confirmed Bulatovic's words. Do you now notice any difference?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, because both of them spoke. First one of them spoke and then the other. Both of them spoke. I did not make a distinction between what the two of them said. Strugar said one thing, Bulatovic said another thing. Strugar continued, Bulatovic followed up. They were the ones who spoke that evening. And this is what transpires from the transcript. When I testified in the Milosevic case, I did not want to point out Strugar as opposed to Bulatovic or vice versa. I just said what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come that in the first statement that you gave to the Prosecution you never mentioned having heard anything like that from General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went without saying. I mentioned Strugar as somebody who was there on behalf of the army, the main person there, and everything applied to Strugar. In any case, when I gave my statement -- allow me. When I gave my statement in Sydney, when I testified in the Milosevic case, I did not make any distinctions. You are trying to make -- to have me make distinctions. At that moment, I did not pay any attention as to who was the first to speak, whether it was Strugar or whether it was Bulatovic. You may draw your own conclusions. I only said what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that in your statement given in 2001, you didn't mention Pavle Strugar within that context. The statement, I'm sorry, was given in 2000. And you never mention Pavle Strugar saying that there were 30.000 Ustashe. This is what I don't find in the statement, and you cannot explain to me how come you didn't say that to the investigators in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I explained what I'd heard. I'd heard that 30.000 Ustashe were advancing towards Montenegro, and that was the main fact that I said to the persons who arrived to interview me in Sydney. And I don't see any difference between that and between what I said later on and between what I'm saying now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are very obvious differences, and I am saying that you're not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this page 11433 be given an exhibit number, as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D19.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you said during your testimony that three Britons asked to get in contact with General Strugar and Admiral Jokic? If I'm not mistaken, this was in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two or three. I forget how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, please. Is it true that you have also said that you asked Pavle Bulatovic, foreign minister at the time, to enable you a telephone contact, and he put you through in your office, and then you spoke directly with Admiral Jokic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your conversation with Admiral Jokic, did you say that in a telephone conversation, Admiral Jokic had told you that General Strugar was standing next to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to check whether on that occasion, did you personally talk to General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I did through Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, I'm going to come to that. Rest assured, I'm going to come to that. In your statement, on page 22, paragraph 4, you say as follows: "In the Ministry of Defence I was given the telephone numbers for Strugar and Jokic, and I called them without any problems." So you were not put through by Pavle Bulatovic, the minister of the interior. You got the numbers from the Ministry of Defence, and you yourself rang them. What is true? Is what you said in 2000 or what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the year 2000, a mistake was made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that then another mistake?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are a lot of mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This is also an answer. Thank you. During that contact with Jokic, did you in any way talk to Strugar and Jokic, or did you just talk to Jokic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only talked to Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same page, page 22, paragraph 4, you say as follows: "Based on the short conversation that I had with the two of them, it was clear that military operations were not going well. In any case, there was no longer the impertinence that they displayed at the meeting held on the 1st of October." Are you using a plural here, indicating that you spoke to the both of them about the military operations and their course, and that in the conversation with the two of them, there was no longer the impertinence that they displayed on the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not with you. I don't know what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that in this statement to the Prosecution, you made it believe that you talked to both Jokic and Strugar.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It says clearly here that I only spoke to Admiral Jokic and that through Admiral Jokic I also talked to Strugar. I didn't speak directly to Strugar. His thoughts were conveyed to me by Admiral Jokic. And if you will allow me. What I said last time, I'd like to repeat now. Admiral Jokic told me: General Strugar and I are asking you this and that, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said, and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the usher's assistance with distributing this document? I have been quoting different paragraphs from the English statement of this witness given to the Prosecution in the year 2000, so I would like everybody in the courtroom to have it, in order to be able to follow it with a greater ease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you proposing, Mr. Rodic, to be dealing with more of the statement, or have you concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not finished with this statement. There will be a few more questions regarding the parts of the statement given by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because at the moment, Mr. Rodic, can I say, this is very much the discussion we had a few days ago with another witness. I think you have very clearly put to the witness those parts from this statement which you say differ from his evidence, and he has either agreed that it's different or he's disagreed, but there's really no need for us to see the statement to identify the differences. They've been made clear by you. And it's not useful simply to tender the whole statement. It's not necessary to reinforce what you've made in your cross-examination. I would expect that if you continue with any other matters from the statement, it will be the same with them. You make clear what was said in the statement, the witness either agrees that he's right or he was wrong, and that's enough for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, in your statement, on page 22, paragraph 4, you say: "On the 1st of October --" I apologise. Not on the 1st of October. "Jokic asked me whether we could recreate the Republic of Dubrovnik. I told him that it was not possible at all, but I believe that this shows to what extent were these people far away from the reality. But he was so convinced that the Greater Serbia would be created that he would not accept it to withdraw from Dubrovnik without having gained some territories first. He knew that I was against an attack, and I believe that he thought I could help them save face." So when you spoke with the OTP for the first time, you did not mention General Strugar as sitting next to Jokic and asking you questions as well. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I said for the purpose of that statement that Admiral Jokic told me: I'm here together with General Strugar, and I and General Strugar would like to know this and that about the Dubrovnik Republic. And I believe that that is exactly what I said to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again the OTP has made another mistake and they have put words into your mouth?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't do that. I don't know what you are reading from. I know what I said to the OTP. I told them that General Strugar had also been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, you have read this statement, you have put your signature on it, indicating that you agree with everything that it says in this statement, and all of a sudden it turns out that there are so many mistakes in this statement.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not true. I don't know what you are reading from. There are 35 pages of this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are on page 22, paragraph 4. Can you please look at it and tell me whether this paragraph differs from your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 22?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The English version?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the English version. Paragraph 4, which starts with the words: "In the Ministry of Defence, I was given the telephone numbers for Strugar and Jokic."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "I was given the telephone numbers for Strugar and Jokic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So what is not clear? What bothers you here? What is the difference, according to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this differ from your testimony before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any differences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it say here that Jokic told you during this telephone conversation that General Strugar was sitting next to him and that both of them were interested in the creation of the Dubrovnik Republic? Does it say anywhere in your statement that this would be the case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that this is Jokic's and Strugar's telephone and that Jokic asked me about the Dubrovnik Republic, and I confirmed that yesterday when I gave my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here it says Strugar's and Jokic's phone, and now say that you talked to Jokic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, were they both using the same phone? Were they in the same room?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but this was merely an addition to my testimony two days ago. This was an addition I made. I said Jokic told me: General Strugar and I would like your opinion on this or that. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, do you know where Jokic was physically when you made the call to him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at all where in the Dubrovnik and Herzegovina theatre of war, including Montenegro, where each of these people were, Strugar and Jokic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but Jokic told me: I am present, and so is General Strugar. I got put through for the British people to ask to meet him. However, Admiral Jokic told me: General Strugar cannot see anyone. And then he went on to speak about the Dubrovnik Republic. That's the truth of it. I'm not sure if everything was explained with sufficient clarity in 2000. Maybe not all of these things have been written down. But this is an addition I'm trying to make about the course of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you perhaps tailoring your testimony to suit your own needs in your testimony against General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid. I have nothing personally against General Strugar to be tailoring this testimony to suit any needs. I'm merely telling you the truth and there's nothing else. I am certainly not doing any of the things that you're insinuating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your statement is full of errors.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well be the case, but what you're talking about now contains no errors whatsoever. Here you have Strugar's and Jokic's phone number. I spoke on the phone to Admiral Jokic. And according to what Admiral Jokic said, at least, General Strugar was sitting next to him. There's no discrepancy there. You can draw as many conclusions as you like based on that, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your view.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be my view, but what you are presenting is your own view too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 7, passage 5 of the English statement, you say: "I told Bulatovic that we should convince Croatia that we have no hostile intentions about Croatia. He agreed and proposed that I write a letter that he would later signed and that I could then bring to Zagreb. I visited Zagreb in the summer of 1991, and I met several Croatian government officials, including President Tudjman. I tried to convince them that Montenegro was no threat to Croatia and that our friendship was a long one." Is this correct? Briefly, please, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 10, passage 3, you say: "While I was in The Hague...", the reference is to the 7th of September, 1991, "...Hrvoje Kacic, a friend of mine and a member of the foreign policy committee of the Croatian parliament, told me that the JNA would attack Dubrovnik. I refused to believe this and I tried to convince him that this could never happen." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 10, passage 4, you say: "We returned to The Hague on the 12th of September. I gave a speech, saying that Montenegro was no threat to Croatia, which I sincerely believed at the time." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 12, passage 3: "On the 1st of October, 1991, Lord Carrington's assistant, the Dutch diplomat Henri Wejnaendts came to Podgorica to check whether any Montenegrins had left for the Dubrovnik front to fight there. I tried to convince him that Montenegro could never attack Croatia which I sincerely believed, and everything I told him was in good faith." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 10, passage 3, you say: "I persistently claimed that Montenegro would never attack Croatia. I was probably deeply convinced, having made such promises to Kacic and Wejnaendts. I did it in good faith." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Montenegro attack Croatia or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are familiar with the initiative by the Montenegrin Assembly presented in October to the Croatian parliament concerning the borders between Montenegro and Croatia in relation to the conclusions adopted by the Montenegrin Assembly. This has been tendered into evidence. These are conclusions dated the 8th of October. You were asked this during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the one who actually drafted the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In the statement of reasons, passage 2, it reads: "It has been stated that the Republic of Montenegro is not at war with the Republic of Croatia, nor has any claim on its territory, the reservists from Montenegro in the Dubrovnik area and Herzegovina are members of the JNA. The JNA is in charge of their deployment and their presence there. Therefore, it can't be stated that Montenegro has carried out any acts of aggression against Croatia." This is from the statement of reasons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll go on with this to remind you. You're probably aware of this. In Zarko Domljan's answer on the 15th of October, 1992, in the Croatian parliament, Zarko Domljan is addressing the president, saying -- first of all, he confirms that he has received these documents entitled "initiative," the statement of reasons, and the conclusions adopted by the Montenegrin parliament on the 8th of October, 1991. He states: "Certainly, there would be a more favourable climate for negotiations and for this initiative had the initiative been submitted before the beginning of the aggression against the Republic of Croatia launched from the territory of Montenegro. I have to state this with a great deal of regret," he says. In passage 3, it says: "In the conclusions of the parliament dated the 8th of October, 1991, the Croatian parliament did not name the Republic of Montenegro as the aggressor, but rather, the Republic of Serbia and the so-called JNA, or whatever remained of it." How come the Croats don't agree, the Croats who purportedly were under threat from an aggression by Montenegro? They disagree. They are the ones telling you about the JNA, about the federal organs and about how the country is supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are documents by which we are trying to re-establish peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that, but please tell me one thing: The Croats are here clearly telling you that Montenegro carried out no acts of aggression against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was pursuant to an intervention by Hrvoje Kacic. They left out the part saying that Montenegro was the aggressor. I have done -- I did everything within my power to not have Montenegro included as an aggressor. They omitted this on purpose, in order to enable negotiations between Montenegro and Croatia and in order to re-establish peace. This is an exchange of diplomatic notes, aimed at re-establishing peace. Momir Bulatovic, Milo Djukanovic and myself, the Montenegrin government, made an effort here to stop the war operations that were under way at the time. There's no discrepancy and no contradiction there at all, as you're trying to show. Please allow me. These are documents that I drafted myself, and I tried to prove that Montenegro was not at war, although it was. There were reservists from Montenegro in Dubrovnik, there was fighting around Dubrovnik, and it was very difficult to prove that Montenegro was not at war. And yet, the parliament tried to find some sort of a link in order to enable us to have negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Any paramilitary unit from the territory of Montenegro, I mean the JNA, the corps, the operations group, the army, whatever, can it just completely of its own accord leave for Croatian territory and carry out operation, just like that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, "of its own accord"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of its own accord, pursuant to its own initiative, an initiative provided, for example, by General Strugar or as ordered by a politician, for example, Momir Bulatovic, who was then Prime Minister. Can they mobilise a JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, they can't. General Strugar did not move a unit as ordered by Momir Bulatovic. Momir Bulatovic did not have the power in Montenegro at that time to order the army to move on Dubrovnik or to stay where it was. General Strugar had been ordered by the General Staff of the Yugoslav army. The presidency of Yugoslavia and Slobodan Milosevic. That was the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not trying to assume that there was a different chain of command. I know how it worked.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I too know how it worked at the time and what the chain of command was as regards the attack on Dubrovnik. Dubrovnik was attacked by the JNA from the territory of Montenegro and by deploying reservists from Montenegro. That's the truth of the matter and there's no way to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These reservists from Montenegro, regular soldiers and reservists from Montenegro, as well as reservists from Serbia, regular soldiers from Serbia, from Albania, Muslims, were they all part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the fact that Montenegrin reservists were part of the JNA, is that what you base your claim on that Montenegro attacked Croatia? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did say that a while ago.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not precisely what I said. Montenegro carried out an attack on Croatia by using all the units that it had. The Territorial Defence, the reserve forces, all these were used to attack Dubrovnik, and that was the fact. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence is part of the armed forces of the SFRY and under the purview of the unified command; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's under the command of both the Republic and the armed forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To put it simply: Who runs the show?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, have you reached the conclusion, or nearly the conclusion, of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have just a very few questions left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll sit on longer, then, and finish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago I quoted your statement. You agreed that you spoke and that you tried to convince different people in different positions that Montenegro would not attack Croatia. This, however, did happen, the aggression, as you call it. Therefore, my question to you is: Why did you not hand in your resignation? Why did you not step down as foreign minister? You had been let down because you, in your capacity as foreign minister, put in an effort to convince different people in different positions that no such war would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, I am asking you at that time, at that time, according to you, on the 1st of October, the whole thing began. Why, as soon as you saw that -- what you told all those people was not true, why did you not resign?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I believed that I would be able to make a difference, to help stop the war, that I could in some way stop the hostilities around Dubrovnik. I stayed around for a while, but as soon as I realised that there was nothing I could do, I resigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On page 14, passage 2 of your statement, we have the following statement: "At the time when, on the 4th of October, the next government meeting was held, I was already strongly opposed to war. I believed that the only honourable thing for me to do was to step down as government minister. I spoke about this to my good friend, Hrvoje Kacic, and he pleaded with me not to resign, not to step down. He said, word for word: Please, in God's name, don't do this. He believed that I would perhaps be able to affect the course of events." My question is: On the 4th of October, there was no government meeting, which clearly transpires from the minutes that we have seen. Secondly, was it only Hrvoje Kacic that influenced you to remain in your position by saying: Please, in God's name, don't do this? Or did you have anyone over in Montenegro also to consult on this matter?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had this conversation with Hrvoje Kacic, but he was certainly not the only person who contributed to my decision not to resign right away. The situation was difficult, and it was necessary that I remain in my position to try to help as much as I could do put an end to hostilities. And so I did. The document you're referring to now are exactly the initiative that we tried to have at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same page, paragraph 3, page 14 of the English statement, you say: "However, at the meeting held on the 4th of October, I expressed my opposition to war in no uncertain terms. However, no one really seemed interested in what I had to say. In their eyes, everything was running smoothly." You opposed war, and yet, at a government meeting on the 4th of October, we see that no such meeting took place on that date. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held. That's for sure. The fact that you don't have the minutes certainly doesn't concern me. That's your own problem. Meetings were held very frequently in those days, and they weren't weekly meetings, but rather, every two or three days, or perhaps on a daily basis there was a government meeting. I could not attend all the meetings, just some of the meetings, and I would normally come halfway through the meeting, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me briefly, please: When the war started, as you say, on the 1st of October, when and at which specific meeting of the government did you first speak out against war and express your opposition? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can. I spoke at each and every meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th, the 7th, those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Same page, passage 4, you say: "At the next meeting, on the 7th of October, 1991, the same things were reiterated. Also at that meeting, or the previous meeting, the issue of Prevlaka was brought up and used as an excuse for attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting on the 7th, a discussion began surrounding Prevlaka, and there was a difference of opinions. People had different positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. I'm not interested in that. Page 15, passage 4,, you say: "I heard about many other incidents from ministers who shared my disgust for what was going on and who also believed that this was a disgrace for Montenegro." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: Your purported opposition to war on several occasions, why did you not resign at that point, when you realised that no one was taking you into account?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to avoid repetition. I remained in my position because I believed that I could help to stop the war, and that's why I worked on the initiative that you have mentioned. This initiative got off the ground quite well, in fact. Why the whole thing was suddenly stopped, well, that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the initiative stopped? When was it curtailed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 20th of October or thereabouts. I can't remember the exact date. Following Lord Carrington's proposal. Slobodan Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about October 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the period of time that I'm referring to. I was to go to Zagreb, but Bulatovic, pursuant to orders from Belgrade no doubt, prevented me from going, and that's when the initiative ground to a halt. In a different way, it continued in The Hague, when we met President Tudjman. Therefore, this initiative was pursued with great effort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did this meeting with President Tudjman take place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point in October, following the plenary in The Hague. That was after the 18th of October, when Milosevic refused Lord Carrington's plan. And unbeknownst to Milosevic, we met President Tudjman in an tempt to reach some sort of agreement concerning Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not go into that now.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only wanted to know about the time frame.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 18th of October, I believe, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you resign?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed in my resignation on the 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did it take you so long from the interruption of the initiative?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not only about the initiative, but all the other activities aimed at stopping the bloodshed around Dubrovnik and in the whole of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 20, paragraph 3, it says: "On the 26th of May, 1992, Djukanovic received my resignation to the position of the foreign minister in the government. I knew that they were going to replace me anyway. However, Djukanovic did not react to my resignation, and nothing was done to find a replacement for me." Would you not find that double-faced? You knew that you would be replaced anyway, then you resigned. Eventually you were not displaced. It was only in August that your resignation was accepted.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is no hypocrisy. You say I was being hypocritical. I have the text of this resignation, both English and B/C/S. I handed it over to Djukanovic, and the Assembly accepted my resignation at the end of July, when a new minister was appointed. I was [indiscernible]. From the month of May, I had no duties in Montenegro at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end, let me ask you: Is there any reason of private or any other nature, because of which during your testimony, especially in respect of General Strugar, you put forward various speculations, differences in your testimony, as opposed to your statement? Is there any such reason?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no reason at all. This is just a provocation on your part. I don't have anything against General Strugar. I only testified against the vandalism around Dubrovnik, the destruction of the town, the plunder that took place in Konavle, and the shame that happened to Montenegro. I have nothing against General Strugar. On the contrary; I know that he comes from a very honest family, a family that gave lives for the freedom of Yugoslavia. And I'm very, very sorry that I have to testify against him in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the discrepancies between your statement and your testimony before this Trial Chamber, and it's Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case, bearing in mind that differences between your two written statements, the first one to the OTP and the second one to the OTP, and there are very many such differences and major differences, I am saying that you have not been telling the truth in respect of General Strugar. Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There is no second statement to the OTP. There is only the one statement, the 35-page one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Rodic, for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will now break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers. Re-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, where is the General Staff located?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff is located in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were asked in the Milosevic case about the meeting on 1st of October, where I believe the Defence has presented page 11185, the question was put to you: "Who was there? What was discussed?" Did anyone ask you -- did anyone ask you about any particular names or did you simply volunteer whatever came out? Is that the total question, who was there and what was discussed? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Milosevic case, when I was cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. This is Mr. Nice. This is your direct examination. A question was put to you: "Who was there? What was discussed?" And perhaps since it has been presented to the Chamber, in the interests of time, I would just ask you if there was any second thought about your answer. You said: "I came to the meeting late. I wasn't there from the beginning, but towards the end, because President Bulatovic had sent me with Lord Carrington's deputy," et cetera, et cetera. "So when I came into the hall, I was quite shocked. I had never seen a meeting of that kind. There were about 8 military persons, three or four generals at least, wearing war uniforms, and they were sitting at the tables that we would usually sit at when we would have government meetings." Now, did you see any need to mention specific names in response to that question?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any reason to do that. There were generals, and I confirmed that to Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I said that this was the meeting --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated that when you met with the Office of the Prosecution before the testimony in the Milosevic case, you brought to the attention of representatives that Admiral Jokic was not at this meeting, that there was a mistake in the statement. That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you told the Prosecution that, you did not at any time in the course of your testimony say that Admiral Jokic was at that meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... He was not, was he?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is that he wasn't there, and I corrected that as soon as I was able to do that. I corrected it, and I continue to claim that Admiral Jokic was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But you didn't even have to mention his name, because you had already indicated he wasn't there; is our understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. I said once that he had not been there, and that would suffice, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for this inference. It is very important when he said that, whether he said that at the trial, during the pre-trial, as we have been listening for days now, or whether he said it at some other unidentified occasion. I think that this would be a fair question. It transpires that this is either not important at all or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or critical. Could you be specific in your question, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution ask you to come and say: By the way, I wanted to tell you in Court, or I needed to tell you in Court, that Admiral Jokic was not there? Or did you just tell the Prosecution and leave it to the Prosecution?
