utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I spotted the mistake, I said that Admiral Jokic was not present. That was at the first opportunity. And I repeat that Admiral Jokic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you were not asked that in Court, if you were not asked that in Court, did you have to volunteer it, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not volunteer any information, but as soon as I was asked this question --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, for my sake, as well as Mr. Petrovic, could it be clear whether these answers were directed to the visit on this occasion to The Hague --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or the earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, you and I are speaking now of when you came to The Hague to testify. That's what I'm talking about. When you came to The Hague in 2002, in October, to testify, this is the time frame; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the year 2000, I gave my statement in Sydney. Then I came here and I testified in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you corrected, and I believe this is what His Honour Judge Parker wants to make sure. When you told the Office of the Prosecution people that there was a mistake, that was in 2002, when you came to testify, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I said clearly that a mistake had been made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the way that was handled was you were not asked about Admiral Jokic at the meeting, and you didn't say he was at the meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between 2000, when you met with the various personnel, not just the Office of the Prosecution, you indicated that there were some -- I believe host country officials present, which is common when a host country has an interview taken, did you have any contact with the Office of the Prosecutor between then and, let's say, when you came to testify in 2002?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The contacts that I had with the OTP were in Sydney in 2000, and then again when I came here on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nothing in between, or at least nothing of consequence in between?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Between 2000, when you spoke with the various law enforcement personnel in Sydney, and 2002, when you testified, did you have any contact or meaningful contact with the Office of the Prosecution, between that time period?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any special contacts, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Did you even look at a statement? Did you even pick it up? Did you have it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the statement that was drafted in the year 2000. The statement existed. And I immediately spotted some mistakes, and later on when I arrived here in 2002, I pointed to those mistakes when I spoke with the representatives representing Mr. Nice. I told them that there were mistakes and that I would like to correct them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the statement that you read through, or the statement that you were asked about today was in the English language, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was translated from the Serbo-Croatian to the counsel, and I have before me an English text. And there are differences in the translation from English into Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement that was done in Australia was done in English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The one that was drafted in Australia was in English. And here I have received a text in Serbo-Croatian, and I notice some discrepancies between the original and the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the first time you saw your own native-tongue version of the statement, in other words, Serbo-Croatian, was in 2002, when you came to testify?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the final Serbo-Croatian text when I arrived here. In 2000, there were questions in English. I did not have a Serbo-Croatian text in front of me. Even in 2002 I was looking at the English text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although you have a facility to speak English on a certain level, would you characterise your primary linguistic knowledge as being in Serbo-Croatian? Is that your mother tongue? Or Montenegrin, as you may have referred to it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I speak Montenegrin, which is not identical to the Serbo-Croatian, or Croatian and Serbian. That's one thing. Secondly, the statement that I gave in Sydney was in English, which is -- my English is limited. There were some language barriers between me and Mr. Williamson. Mr. Williamson has an accent, a bit different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Now, before, before you were even asked to put your initials on a statement, you had to go through it, but did you go through it in English or did someone read it to you? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was supposed to read it in English. It was in English. I accepted it as such. I was not very attentive. And that's how things started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... not your native tongue?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not my native tongue. I was just out of the hospital, and certainly there were some errors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there were -- and you have been given an opportunity to correct those errors, have you not, since you've come to The Hague, either in 2002 or now?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an opportunity now, and now is when I pointed out certain mistakes. I didn't consider them very important. But it turned out in the end that there were many more mistakes than I originally believed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then 2002, to the extent you could, you pointed out certain mistakes, including the fact that you said Admiral Jokic was not at that meeting on 1 October; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is completely correct. That's what I pointed out when I spoke to the investigators. And I believe I said the same thing on cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if an initial error is made with sort of the team of Strugar and Jokic appearing in one place with reference to a particular meeting, did you find it -- that same mistake carried through every time Strugar was mentioned, at least in terms of that meeting, that, for whatever reason, Jokic's name got added to it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a quick bit of information. Can you just tell us: At the meeting in Sydney, how many people -- were people talking so that there was a lot of conversation coming from different directions?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several people present, and many different questions were asked and facts put forward. It is only natural that errors occurred such as the one which turned up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me a second. In terms of any discussions with relation to Admiral Jokic, you indicated in the Milosevic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to Ms. Somers for interrupting. I just want to ask a question. This is the first time we're facing a situation like this, and there's one thing I want to know: how the Chamber feels about this. When re-examining a witness, is the OTP entitled to ask leading questions, or do we still abide by the same Rule as applies to the examination-in-chief? I want to know about the established practice and about the Chamber's view on this. Therefore, we want to find out if these leading questions asked by the OTP right now by my learned friend and colleague are allowed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want to put any submission, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour. Thank you. I think if I had to take -- first of all, I would ask for some latitude with this witness, given the amount of time he's been on the stand and given the fact that if I had to go back and cite every single page or every single reference, we would have an interminable examination. I think there's no abusive practice, in that these questions were effectively raised during cross, and I'm trying to get a clarification so that the Chamber's concerns, which were noted, are addressed. I have to direct his attention to certain matters anyway, and it may -- it may end up that it comes off perhaps appearing to be leading, when in fact he may have the answer directly coming out of his own mouth. But I would ask for, if the Chamber is viewing it in this direction, some latitude here. I think it would be warranted in this circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the normal position is leading questions are not appropriate in re-examination. It is necessary, though, for speed and everybody's convenience, for the counsel to direct the attention of the witness to particular issues or particular answers that were given in the course of cross-examination. And in that respect, there is often an appearance of leading. But having got the witness's attention directed to the issue that will be the subject of the question, the question then should not be a leading question. Ms. Somers has been sliding either side of the line there, as she has gone along, and I'm sure with your intervention she will be more conscious of keeping on the right side of the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We accept that, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- reasons for doing that under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement -- and you may not have memorised the portion, and if you don't remember it, I would ask you to let me know, and I would ask the Chamber to allow you perhaps to refresh your recollection. But when you spoke of General Strugar's comments at the meeting of 1 October, whether or not the term "30.000" was in the same paragraph, which is what counsel has raised to you on cross-examination. Do you recall any mention -- do you recall any mention about General Strugar's actual comment in the paragraph, or in the portion where you said that -- you talked about his enthusiasm for defending Yugoslavia? Do you recall what you may have said specifically? And if you don't, again, please tell me, and I will ask the Chamber if it would allow you to refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he said what I said, that 30.000 Ustasha were advancing on Montenegro and that we should defend ourselves. When I walked into the meeting, Strugar was saying this. Momir Bulatovic spoke after him, and then Strugar spoke again, and then Momir Bulatovic, and then the remaining ministers present. That was the course of the meeting, and the meeting was already halfway through, if not even further along. I was late to the meeting because I had just returned from Cetinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It appears that exact memory is not on point, and I would ask the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you if it would help you as to what exactly you told the investigators at the time to look at your statement. Would it help you to remember better if you looked?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can I please have the statement? It's been four years since I made the statement. Therefore, I think I should be allowed to have a look. I don't think I said anything special that I wouldn't be able to remember today as for what happened at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to hand, if it's permissible -- it is page 12 in English of 35. And I don't have the B/C/S cite. Perhaps I can just find that as well. If you'd give me one second. And it would be on page 12 of the English, and it would be on page 11 of the Serbo-Croatian version. Do you have both, Mr. Usher? Okay. If I may -- just to draw the attention. It's ERN, in the Serbo-Croatian edition, it's page 11, and it's ERN 03013957. If I may offer the usher as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Serbo-Croatian, I have -- just in order in the interest of time, put a mark alongside in yellow to direct your attention to the paragraph. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Does that help you as to the comment regarding --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If I could -- now, having --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that's not correct is: Jokic as inserted. Now that's an error, and it's an error that I wish to correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. We're looking right now -- you have made that correction and we very much appreciate that. But when you were asked -- the comment about the term "Ustasha" and General Strugar, can you remember what you said now that you've had a chance to refresh your recollection? What was your comment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustasha is a derogatory term for --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Samardzic. Let's make sure we understand each other. And I will - again, if the interests of the Chamber would permit me to - direct you to the particular passage that just helped you refresh your recollection. Strugar said he was happy that the Montenegrins would fight. He said that the JNA would defend Yugoslavia against aggression by the Ustasha and that the Dubrovnik -- and Dubrovnik would be liberated at a minimum cost. He added that there were many Ustasha there. Now, is that the reference to the numbers that you have attributed in that particular passage to General Strugar addressing, "many Ustasha"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That there were a large number of Ustasha in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then just below, there's a reference to -- I'm sorry. Excuse me one second. Just above it, I beg your pardon, there's a reference to Bulatovic, with the number 30.000. Now, was the comment -- are you linking the two comments? Are you suggesting -- do we understand you correctly that General Strugar affirmed what was said, whether there may have been mutual affirmation by Strugar and Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. 30.000 Ustasha, that refers to what Strugar said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Croatians ever attack Montenegro during this period? Was there in fact the dreaded attack on Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Croatians never attacked Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Nothing further. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow. There are two things that have cropped up in this re-examination that are not connected to the witness, but rather to the work of the Prosecution in this case. What this re-examination indicates is that this witness in his statement prior to testifying in the Milosevic case made certain corrections to his statement. The first question I want to raise is: Is there any written trail of this in the OTP, a document like the one we were given today? Every time an interview is conducted with a witness, there are notes that are taken in one form or another. They are drafted as an additional statement or an internal memorandum for the OTP. Is there any such document? That's my first question. The second question is, and I'm referring to the period prior to the 8th of October, 1991, my second question is: In view of the fact that the witness inserted certain corrections prior to his testimony in the Milosevic case, was the accused, Milosevic, provided with such a document containing the corrections made by Mr. Samardzic to the OTP before he entered the courtroom on the 8th of October, 2002, as has been done in our case? I believe these are both material questions and that there should be a paper trail from the period. Thank you. Of course, by your leave, we would very much like to have these documents and to see what exactly he stated in them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, there is -- any meetings between the OTP and the witness, if anything new is brought up, it is in some way dealt with, either through testimony or however the particular Prosecutor in question deems most appropriate. So that particular issue is a matter that was handled by that Prosecution team. The second question is, it is unclear why Mr. Petrovic is particularly concerned about the Milosevic receipt of anything. But I'm confident that if there is any addendum to be made or any correction to be made, this transcript will be provided to the Milosevic team. It is public testimony. And it will certainly make its way where appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. I think you misunderstand the point, Ms. Somers. Mr. Petrovic is concerned whether there is any verification in writing of the evidence -- that before giving evidence in the Milosevic trial, Mr. Samardzic indicated corrections that should be made, and if so, he would like to see that. And there were two limbs to that. Firstly, the general, and then the particular question: Did that paper trail take the form of a written correction, such as was used in this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I cannot address the paper aspect of it for another group of Prosecutors, and if the second prong is would it have been -- again, they would be dependent on another group of persons. But the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder whether I could ask you, if it is practical to identify any paper record, to make it available. If it is not practical to identify it, we will have to proceed on the basis that there is no paper record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We'll make an inquiry of the other persons involved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did I correctly understand your concern, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, of course, Your Honour. I'm not in the least interested in the Milosevic case, as far as that aspect is concerned. What I want to know is whether there was any such thing there. Even more importantly, if there was no such thing, how should Ms. Somers know that today, on the basis of what, if something was done back in 2002, how is it that she was informed about it if there is no paper trail? This is a very simple matter, I believe, Your Honour, and we are adamant that we should be given the specific document in which this is stated. And as far as such a document exists from 2002, October, or whenever Mr. Samardzic claims that he made these corrections to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the existence of a paper trail, just so that it's clear, is by no means essential. If we learn of a correction that needs to be made, or if it appears from testimony that there is something that needs to be corrected, we will inquire of each other. But we are always very interested to make sure that at least to the extent possible, that the witness lets us know of anything that is not right, and again, may be dealt with by different Prosecutors in different ways. This is the way I have dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, so that we're all clear, it's left on the basis that you will cause inquiries to be made. If you can identify a paper record, you will make it available. If you do not, we will proceed on the basis that there is no paper record. We will be --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I just raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic is still here, I believe, for a bit of time, and should there need to be any matter addressed by the other Prosecution team, I'm sure that VW would make him available. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention that we will adjourn now for the day. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00. When we resume, there are two matters that we think it would be convenient to deal with shortly but immediately. Each concern expert witnesses. Firstly, we wish to hear the brief Defence submissions concerning the general question of expert witnesses and their statements, that we were hoping to hear last week, but there proved not to be time to do it. The second issue is that I understand now in your schedule, Ms. Somers, you will be reaching, you expect, an expert witness near the end of this week, and we would appreciate some brief submissions on the relevance of the evidence of that witness to the issues in the indictment. And if there's anything in response to that, also from Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were served with a motion about this, and we would seek to respond to it, and I think -- so the Defence has already filed, and it would be our -- it was our expert, their response under 94 bis, and then we'd seek to reply. So we'll get that to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would hope to hear you orally in the morning first thing on those two issues. Thank you. We will adjourn now for the day. Mr. Samardzic, I do beg your pardon. I was rude enough to ignore you. I didn't mean to do that. May we thank you for your attendance and for the evidence and assistance that you've given to us, and you are now free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
